intro: You're looking for a child arrangements solicitor near you because you need help with where your children live or how often they see each parent. Whether you're trying to reach an agreement or facing a court application, a solicitor can explain your options and guide you through the process. We introduce you to a UK solicitor who handles child arrangements, and they will quote you directly.
need_heading: What people searching for a child arrangements solicitor usually need
need_lead: Most people want clear, practical advice on sorting out contact and living arrangements in a way that puts their children first.
needs: You and your ex-partner disagree about where the children should live and need help finding a workable solution.
You want to set up a regular pattern of contact but the other parent is refusing to discuss it.
You're worried about your child's safety or wellbeing during contact and need advice on protecting them.
You've been invited to a mediation information and assessment meeting and want to understand what it involves before you go.
You're considering applying to court for a child arrangements order and need to know what the process involves.
context_heading: One key thing to understand about child arrangements
context: Before most court applications about child arrangements, you'll usually need to attend a mediation information and assessment meeting (MIAM) unless an exemption applies. The court's main concern is the welfare of the child, and it will expect you to have tried to agree arrangements where it's safe to do so. A solicitor can explain how this works in your situation.

Solicitors in England and Wales are regulated by the Solicitors Regulation Authority (SRA), and you can check an individual or firm on the SRA's register. In Scotland, solicitors are regulated by the Law Society of Scotland, and in Northern Ireland by the Law Society of Northern Ireland. Regulated firms must hold professional indemnity insurance and have a complaints procedure; if that doesn't resolve things, the Legal Ombudsman can look at service complaints in England and Wales.
tell_heading: What to tell iComply when you enquire
tell: The ages of your children and where they currently live.
What you and the other parent have already tried to agree, and what the sticking points are.
Whether there are any safety concerns, such as domestic abuse or substance misuse, that affect contact.
Whether you've already been to a mediation information and assessment meeting or received any court forms.
Your location, so we can introduce you to a solicitor near you.
Any deadlines you're working towards, such as a court date or a response date on an application.
questions: What experience do you have with child arrangements cases like mine?
Will I need to attend a mediation information and assessment meeting before we can apply to court?
How will you keep my child's welfare at the centre of the advice?

faqs.q: Do I have to go to mediation before I can apply to court about child arrangements?
faqs.a: In most cases, you'll need to attend a mediation information and assessment meeting (MIAM) before making a court application, unless an exemption applies. The meeting is a chance to find out whether mediation could help you reach an agreement without going to court.

faqs.q: How can I check that a solicitor is properly regulated?
faqs.a: In England and Wales, you can check a solicitor or firm on the Solicitors Regulation Authority (SRA) register. In Scotland, check with the Law Society of Scotland, and in Northern Ireland with the Law Society of Northern Ireland. This helps you confirm they are authorised to carry out reserved legal work.

faqs.q: What does the court consider when deciding child arrangements?
faqs.a: The court's main concern is the welfare of the child. It will look at factors such as the child's wishes and feelings, their physical and emotional needs, and the ability of each parent to meet those needs. A solicitor can explain how these factors might apply in your case.

faqs.q: Can a solicitor help me communicate better with my ex-partner about the children?
faqs.a: Yes, a solicitor can help you set up clear, child-focused communication and may suggest ways to reduce conflict, such as using a parenting plan or mediation. They can also correspond with the other parent on your behalf if that helps.

extra_heading: Choosing between the child arrangements solicitors you find nearby
extra: Searching for a child arrangements solicitor near me usually means you want someone you can actually get to, whether that's for an initial appointment or for meetings as matters progress. Distance matters less than it once did, though, because much of the work can be handled by phone, email or video, so it's worth asking how each solicitor prefers to work before you rule anyone out on location alone.

When you compare the options we introduce you to, look at how each one handles children's cases specifically, rather than family law in general. Ask what proportion of their work involves child arrangements, how they approach encouraging agreement before court, and how they would keep communication child-focused if relations with your ex-partner are strained. Their answers will tell you more than any description of the firm.

Remember that the quote you receive is a starting point rather than a fixed sum, since the work depends on how much is in dispute and whether court becomes necessary. Ask each solicitor to explain how their fees are structured and what might cause costs to rise, so you can compare like with like. It's also worth confirming that whoever will handle your matter is a solicitor or another authorised professional, as the word lawyer alone isn't protected.

extra_faqs.q: Does it matter if the child arrangements solicitor is not on my doorstep?
extra_faqs.a: Not necessarily. Many child arrangements matters are handled largely by phone, email and video, and court papers can be dealt with remotely. What matters most is that the solicitor understands your situation and that you can communicate with them comfortably.

extra_faqs.q: What should I expect at a first appointment about child arrangements?
extra_faqs.a: The solicitor will usually ask about your children, where they live now, what you and the other parent have already tried, and whether there are any safety concerns. They should then explain your options, including mediation and the court process, and set out how their fees work. It helps to bring any relevant letters or court forms with you.

extra_faqs.q: Can I speak to more than one solicitor before deciding?
extra_faqs.a: Yes, and it can be sensible to do so, since fees and approach vary between firms. We can introduce you to a suitable solicitor and they will quote you directly, so you can weigh up the options before committing to anyone.
